What might they do?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why do so many stories show a character who is less powerful than the people around them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Because it's something a lot of people worry about. Under each root, write the unit words and circle the root in each: trans- (transformation, transition), mort- (immortal, mortals), -tion (isolation, revelation, transformation)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Words are built from parts. If I know the part, I can make a smart guess about a new word. Look at immortal: im- means not, and mort- means death. So immortal means not able to die. Now look at mortals. Same root, no im-. What might mortals be?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Mortals are people who can die, so regular humans. It's the opposite of immortal, like the gods in myths."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Percy feels cut off from everyone at school. Which word with -tion could name that feeling, and how does the suffix help you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Isolation. The base is isolate, which means to set apart, and -tion turns it into the noun for the state of being alone."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Percy's story may hold a transformation, a big change, and maybe a revelation, a surprise that gets revealed. You can use these words in your paragraph if they fit, but only if they are accurate."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"The cap for this lesson is six words. If time is short, teach trans-, mort-, and -tion with one word each and leave the rest on the chart for later reference. Keep the chart posted all unit."}]},{"id":"lab-decode-names","title":"Word Study 2: Decoding Long Names and Terms","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.2","L.6.6"],"routine":"Syllable Chunking","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Choose a long name or term from Chapter 1 or from the Hare excerpt. Try Soongoora: Soon / goo / ra. Try a long term such as immortal: im / mor / tal. The mort- chunk shows up in the middle."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What helps you check that you split the word in a way that sounds right?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Each chunk has a vowel sound, and when I put the chunks back together it sounds like a real word I've heard, or the teacher says it the same way."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Say the Hare excerpt names aloud yourself first so students hear the model. Do not mock or rush mispronunciations. Have the class repeat chunk by chunk."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students gather evidence from both texts, compare how Percy and Soongoora respond to powerful figures, and write an explanatory paragraph with a clear topic sentence, evidence, transitions, precise language, and a concluding statement.","activities":[{"id":"lia-model-explanatory","title":"Review and Model Explanatory Writing","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","W.6.2.f"],"routine":"Teacher Modeling","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"An explanatory paragraph has three jobs. First, a topic sentence that tells the reader exactly what you will explain. Second, relevant evidence, which means details from the text that prove your point, and an explanation of how each one connects. Third, a concluding statement that follows from what you said and says why it matters. Transitions such as similarly, in contrast, for example, and as a result keep it smooth."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Here is a model on a different topic so I do not give you your answer. Topic sentence: Both a library and a park give people a place to belong. Evidence: In the library, people share books and quiet tables. Similarly, in the park, neighbors share benches and games. Conclusion: As a result, both places remind people that a community is built by sharing space. Notice the topic sentence names the idea, each detail proves it, and the last sentence explains why it matters."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words in the model show comparison, and which sentence is the concluding statement?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Similarly shows the comparison. The last sentence starting with As a result is the conclusion because it tells what the examples mean."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners recognize the parts of an explanatory paragraph and the language that signals each part.","sayAsk":"Point to each part of the model and have students echo its name.
